If I thought that my action was construed in that way by those who have moved this resolution-I know it is not-I would not- I would not vote for the resolution at all, because Ontario is the only power that can
deal with this question. Some person may say to me-I have seen the insinuation in some newspapers in Quebec and in some in Ottawa that the Ontario Government is made up of bigots and fanatics, and that the legislature in general is of the same calibre. I have no brief for the Ontario Government, as .you can weli understand; hut I know Premier Hearst, and nobody can make me believe that Hearst has the least semblance of a bigot in his make-up. I am acquainted with the man. I know the Hon. Thomas McGarry, and I know him to he broadminded, a man who- hews to the line and tries to do the right thing. I was associated for years with the Hon. W. J. Hanna in the Provincial Legislature, and there is not a man in Canada who can make me believe that Hanna is a fanatic, or has the semblance of a fanatic in his anatomy, or is a man who would do anything wrong as between men in the way of encroaching upon their rights. These men are not bigots. These men have a duty to perform. But, lest I may he misunderstood-I have mentioned only three because they are the three I know best-the others, I have every Teason to believe, are in 11 p.m. the same category. Coming to the Opposition, I know N. W. Rowell. Rowell is not a bigot; he is one of the broadest-minded men in the Dominion, and one of the Ablest men as well. I know many of his followers who were in the Ontario Legislature when I was there. I know Charles Bowman, a man of German descent, who, like his father, is a credit to the province of Ontario. There is not an iota of bigotry in the make-up of Mr. Bowman. Another I think of is Mr. Sam. Clark, of Cobourg, a man of all men, open-hearted, broadminded, and with a heart that would take in everybody in the Dominion of Canada and have some room left. This question must not he discussed on the supposition that the men in the Ontario Government or in the Ontario Legislature are narrowminded. I do not admit that; I resent it, because, knowing these men, I know they do not view their public duty from that standpoint.
Let me deal for a moment with the question of disallowance. I need not say that I am not in favour of the disallowance of this Act. There have been very few Acts passed the disallowance of which I would favour. Sir Allen Aylesworth, Minister of Justice in the former Government, once made the statement that in his opinion a

province had a right to do wrong if it wanted to. That was possibly putting it broadly, but to a large extent, the powers given to the provinces under the Act of Confederation enables them to do that, so long as some great public right is not interfered with. I know of legislation for the disallowance of which petitions came to the federal authority in the time of the Administration of my right hon. leader that bore upon their face evidences of injustice. The Minister of Justice then took the ground that the people of Ontario had the power to punish a Government that would pass that kind of a law and that the matter was their business and not ours. I think that is fairly sound logic and sound constitutional practice, although the law would allow them to take another view. But, there is another reason in this case why I would be absolutely against disallowance. If the grievance now claimed does really exist, disallowance would not help one iota. Those of us who are older remember the disallowance of provincial Acts many years ago, with what result, Sir? These Acts wena immediately re-enacted by the Ontario Legislature, disallowed again, and re-enacted again, until they went to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. No real remedy could be afforded, particularly in a case of this kind, by disallowance. It would only add to the irritation, and the Government did exactly right in not thinking of disallowing,, this Act. Further than that, they would have been compelled to take the strong ground that 'this Act was so injurious that it should be disallowed, although it was absolutely within the purview of the Ontario Legislature, which nobody does dispute, or nobody can dispute, if he looks upon the matter dispassionately.
But you say: " Then, that being the case, this question should have been referred to the courts and finally decided." If this were a question of commerce, if this were a question of some minor importance, -of something that dealt only with the heads ,and not the hearts of people, I would say that a decision by the courts would settle it. But this is a question far and beyond and above anything in the way of a commercial transaction or of a commercial dispute. It is something that touches the beings of men, something that touches their history and their traditions, and no decision of any court, no matter what it may be, can alleviate the irritation that exists. I say to those who are prosecuting that case and taking it to the courts that, no matter what 
the decision may be, the people of Ontario will have to deal with the question ultimately.
May I ask the hon. gentleman if he means that it would be desirable to test the opinion of the country at large upon this matter?

I am not objecting to it, but I do not suggest it. My hon. friend has a constituency where he thinks . he could use this question fairly well, as he did the ne temere decree. I say that a decision of the court, no matter on which side it was, would not alleviate the condition or remove the irritation. Why do I say that? Supposing that those who make the complaint of this law were upheld and the decision were in their favour, * think you that, if the Ontario Legislature did not believe in the justice or wisdom of the decision, they would not and could not find a hundred ways of getting around it without violating it? Everyone knows that. They need not pass any legislation to implement the decision. They could do several things, refuse to grant money and that kind of thing. That would not help. I say to the French people of Ontario : suppose the decision were against you, then where would you be? I am not a lawyer, but my judgment is that if the case goes to court it will be decided in favor of the Ontario government. This being so, an appeal to the courts would not lessen the irritation; it would but add to it, no matter what the decision might be.
What is the only remedy? You say to me: ''Why should we have anything to do with this question in the federal Parliament"? That has been decided by almost the unanimous vote of the House, and I will not discuss it. But, if there be a grievance, I do not know. Is it claimed that there is a grievance? It is. If any man imagines that he has a grievance, he is as much troubled in his heart as if he had a real grievance, because to him it is a real grievance. One thing I do know is that for some reason hundreds of children to whom we owe an education are walking the streets, or have been, and are not getting it. I do not know what the situation is to-day. We owe-'a duty to these children, and those on either side who are preventing an arrangement being brought about by which these children can proceed on their course to manhood and womanhood are taking a grave responsibility. There is a grievance, or an alleged grievance, I am not sure which it is. It exists in the minds of a lot of people

at least, and we in Ontario ought to be big enough to find some way to do justice to the children of Ontario if not to the children in the other parts of the country. What is to be that way? It cannot be by law, it cannot be by coercion, it cannot be by disallowance, it cannot be by court decision ; it must be through some friendly and conciliatory method on the part of both parties. It will not do to say: "You have no grievance; there is the law." That makes no difference to the man who thinks he has a grievance. iStoniething ought to be done. Are we not big enough in Ontario to devise a method 'by which a remedy can be found?
I said that I did not know whether there was a just cause for a grievance or not. This much I do know, that, having sat in this House, I have heard men, learned in the law, on each side if the House say there is no cause for a grievance be- . cause the amendment to the Ontario law does not mean that those who claimed to have a grievance insist it does mean. The acting Minister of Education said that these amendments to the Act are not intended to deprive children of French-speaking parents of any privilege they had. Mr. Rowell has said the same thing. Their remarks appeared in the same newspapers. That is the Ontario side of it. Hon. gentlemen in this House have said the same thing. Eminent men on this side of the House, whose ability both as statesmen and lawyers no person will question, declare just as emphatically that these amendments can bear an interpretation which does deprive the children of French-speaking parents of the privileges that they have always enjoyed. Who is right? I do not know. There should be some person to say who is right as between these two opinions. I know a most eminent lawyer in Canada who has said that this Regulation 17 is weak, and if it is apparently capable of two constructions, surely there is some method by which that weakness can be removed and the law made clear so that there can be no dispute that it means what the Ontario Government and legislature say it means, xf that be done the cause of grievance is removed, so far as I am concerned. If some enactment can toe passed that will make it so clear that lawyers cannot differ, and everybody will know that this legislation means what the Ontario Government says it means, there will be no cause, I think, for the grievance among those who are now complaining. Lawyers may laugh
at that, but lawyers make good fees out of these very differences. If these differences did not get into legislation we should have fewer lawyers. Not being of that profession myself, I cannot appreciate these technicalities but I do know that they exist. Prominent legal men have said to me that the interpretation put upon these amendments by the leader of the Opposition and by the horn, member for Kamour-aska is not a strained one. Now, this resolution only suggests, nothing more. It does not ask; it does not adviise; it merely expresses the opinion that, that being the case, it would be wise if all doubt were removed by having the legislation of Ontario made so clear that nobody could say that it did not mean what the Ontario Government says it means. That is not a very big demand. Knowing the members of the Ontario Government, I believe that if the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Prime Minister, the Minister of Finance, the member for East Toronto, and the member for South Toronto-Ontario men, who have the right to sit down and discuss it directly with the Ontario Government-I believe that if they were to sit down and discuss this matter with Premier Hearst, this grievance would be removed in twenty-four hours. I know the men of whom I 'speak, and I say in all fairness to the members of the Ontario Government that I *have never found any of them showing the least symptom of bigotry, or a desire to interfere with amy man on account of his religion or origin. That being true, I urge upon the Government and the members from Ontario the wisdom of sitting down quietly with the members of the Ontario Government, and pointing out that *if they will make clear what they say is their intention, much of t'he trouble will be removed. If that can be done-and it seems to mfe very simple-there will have been accomplished by this discussion, conducted as it has been without any irritation, harshness or abuse, something that will be worth all the money that has been expended in the holding of this session of Parliament, if it accomplished nothing else. Let ns look at our hearts at the present moment. The greatest necessity in this hour, in the face of an enemy who has appeared almost unbeatable, is that all hearts in iCanada should beat as one. If friendly conference by men from Ontario with the authorities in Ontario can bring about a state of affairs whereby the present friction, no matter from what cause, will



no longer exist, and hundreds of children . now going uneducated will return to the schools, and we in -Canada, no matter from what part we come or what our race or origin, -can say that we have no grievance against each other, we shall be in a better position than we have been in for the last eighteen months to face and overcome the enemy, because the people of the Empire will be united.

speakeroldname: Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a very few words -to say in connection with the question that has been debated now for two days, -and the discussion of which, I suppose, is now nearing its end.
I have listened attentively to every speech that has been made, including the speech which has ibeen made by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat (Mr. Graham); and I -acknowledge to this House and to myself that now, just at this moment, I -am more mystified as to why this resolution was ever brought here than I have been at any other time during this debate. I have been trying to find out what it was brought here for, I have diligently scanned the arguments, and listened to most of them as they have proceeded from those who have spoken; and I cannot yet see, from anything that has been said by my right hon. friend who is the father of the resolution, or by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat-taking them as the two principal exponents-what in the wide world this resolution was ever brought here for, if it was not brought here for mischief. It seems to -me like the foolish prank o-f a -mischievous boy. My hon. friend who has just taken his seat spoke of firebrands. He has been on tenterhooks ever since this resolution came into this House lest some word should be spoken which would set a fire going that would blaze up all over this country. Was it necessary, in order to make a protest to the Ontario Government, that you should contemplate firebrands and- conflagrations, and bring tinder into this House which would contribute to it?
IMy right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) says: "I do not want to dictate; I have not the -least idea of giving Ontario advice; all I want to do is to make a plea and have a hearing." Good gracious, Mr. -Speaker'! Could he not have made the same ple-a without a resolution? Could not everybody in this House have said what everybody 
has said on a motion to go into Supply, without bringing in any resolution at all as an amendment to that motion? Then why was the resolution brought? That is what mystifies me. How is it with the rest of you on each side of this House?
It synchronizes.

There is another thing which shows the absurdity of trying to try out a question of this kind in a forum which is uninformed, and cannot possibly be informed on the very kernel of the question. My hon. friend from Nico-let (Mr. Lamarche), in that excellent speech of his -as to form and clearness, although jl do not agree with everything he has said here this afternoon, charged the Ontario Government with various wrongdoings. Who is there here to answer for the Ontario -Government? Is the Ontario Government at the bar of this House when charges are made that deeply affect its honour, its s-pirit of -fairness, and its objects? Is there any one at the bar of this House to speak on behalf of the Ontario Government, to give the reason for its acts, to explain what is not -clear or defend what is wrongly attacked? I am satisfied that there is an answer to every charge that has been made; but no man in this House who has not grown up in the atmosphere of the Ontario Legislature, who has not gone from an Ontario constituency to enact the legislation which' pertains to that House under our -Constitution, no -matter how able he is, can take up a question like this, which has a growth of thirty	years in the province,	andbe at even advantage with reference to it, know	its genesis,	its	developmentand the	truth that	ie	in it.	Alawyer can	take a brief	and	make a	very
good case out of it; but there is no man on either side of this House-and the debate we have had here has shown it-who is capable of taking this educational problem, that has been before the Legislature of Ontario and the various Governments of Ontario for these many years, and thoroughly understanding it, can do it justice or speak with authority with reference to it. So almost every man who has spoken has had a different idea of its purport, none know certainly.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition is consumed with a spirit which impels him to make a plea. To what God is he praying? If he wants to make a plea which shall be an effective one, let

him put his plea upon the altar of the being who is able to grant it or refuse it. My right hon. friend the other night seemed to be under the impression that such a deity was my hon. friend who sits here by my right (Mr. Eogers). At the very end of one of his most impassioned pleas, he said, turning to my hon. friend: "Will you grant me that?" The man to whom he ought to have gone was that good, fair, impartial man, Mr iHearst, the (Premier of Ontario, by long knowledge of whom my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) felt himself justified in saying with reference to 'him:
He is no bigot; he is an honest man who tries to do even justice to every one in his province."
I am afraid my hon. friend is going further than I said.

That is the man to whom you should have gone with your plea, and not to my hard-hearted though large-hearted friend who comes from Manitoba. That is the one thing that seems to me to show the absurdity of bringing this question here, where there is nobody to answer for it or to say whether or not he can or will grant the plea.
Row, ;I want to pick a bone with my hon. friend (Mr. Graham). In the interest of the very people whom he has been championing here to-night, was it a fair estimate to make of that French-Canadian character which began to develop upon the shores of Canada 150 years ago, for him to say that because a French child some-v.here in Ontario is alleged, for a little while, in learning grammar and geography, to be kept from using his own language or having his own language uttered to him, therefore that grand race shall refuse to fight for the country that they have adopted and the country that they love? I have formed no such opinion of my French Canadian friends in this House or in this country of Canada, and I think that my hon. friend was ill-advised when he supposed that before you could get recruits in Quebec you must fix up this small trouble on the streets of Ottawa, where the children aTe pacing the streets instead of being in the schools-on account of whose fault? . Because somebody chose to be disobedient to the law-nothing less and nothing more than that. The greatest crime that a man can commit in a democratic country is to refuse to obey the laws that the democracy imposes upon him.

That is what I said.
239i

That is done in the streets of Ottawa; and yet I have not heard a single expression of regret as to that side of the question .from my right hon. friend who had so much to say with reference to the faults of many people in Ontario.
My hon. friend from Nicolet (Mr. La-marche) uttered, I think, a heresy this afternoon when he stated that the law should not be appealed to, that the courts should not be appealed to, in order' to get rid of a law which was oppressive, because by doing so you proclaimed your adhesion to the law. There are only three ways of getting rid of a law.' One is to go to the law-giver and convince him that the law is an improper one and get him to amend it or to get it out of the way.
Hear, hear.

My hon.
friend said: "hear, hear". A brave man and a man who honestly wants to get what he says he wants to get goes to the man who has the power of giving it, and does not stand three or four hundred miles off and make long shots through a foreign substance and wait until by similar long shots in the opposite direction, he gets a reply from somebody who has nothing to do with the matter. In my boyhood days, if I wanted something from my mother, I went straight to her and asked her for' it and I got it; I did not run around to all the Aunt Sallys in the. neighbourhood.
The other ways of getting rid of an obnoxious law is either to have it annulled in the courts if it is illegal or to reverse it through the electors.
There was another little heresy of my hon. friend, and I think a heresy uttered by one or two others, including the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. iE. Lapointe). Just here let me state what I thought while this debate was going on. If I were a young man like some of those Englishspeaking men, around me, I would study from this very moment straightforward until I could speak French just as well as some of my French friends speak English in this House. The ability to speak two languages gives a man power. I am, however digressing a little; what I wanted to do was to compliment my hon. friend from Kamouraska on the excellent English in which he addressed himself to his subject. My hon. freind, however, as to that little heresy of his, has taken comfort to himself and solace for his conscience in try-

mg to find a reason for the bringing of this question into this House. "We have a right to bring it here", he says; and it is here properly, because the Speaker said they had the right to bring it here.
I said more than that.

I remember a lesson of my Sunday-sehool days to the effect that there are some things that are right, but which may not be expedient. Some scripture character gave utterance to that many long years ago. Because the Speaker said that under the rules of Parliament, when a motion is made to go into Supply you can bring in an amendment with regard to almost anything under the sun, that does not excuse my hon. friend from bringing in a firebrand motion; and I think he felt a little of that fire burning in his own conscience when he turned to the Speaker's decision and the support given to the Speaker in this House as a solaoe to him for having this firebrand question brought into this House.
My hon. friend, perhaps, does not mean to toe unfair-[DOT]
I will not be unfair.

I was answering the argument of the hon. member for South Toronto (Mr. Macdonell) that we were trying to do something in the way of giving advice or instruction to the Ontario Legislature which we should not do, and I read the paragraph of the Speaker's ruling based on the fact that we were merely asked to express an opinion. I did not give the reasons that the hon. gentleman has given at all.
I accept the hon. gentleman's explanation and if I have done him an injustice I am sorry for it. But the hon. gentleman said he would rather the resolution were not here. Why did he say that? .
For the same reason that I said a good many other things-because it is true.

It is true my hon. friend would rather it was not. iiere. Will he say that, in order to make the plea which he has made, a very effective and straightforward plea, it was necessary that this motion should have been introduced? Could not he have said every word he has said even if this resolution had not been introduced.

Does my hon. friend
want an answer?
Yes.

That answer was given
in almost the next sentence I spoke, when I said that as a citizen of Ontario I would have preferred to go elsewhere to discuss this matter, and I intended to do it. But, as it is here, I propose to support it.

What kind of
a soldier is my hon. friend, to load himself up with unnecessary impedimenta when he goes into the field? He could have done all the fighting he had to do without this resolution. He did not wish it, he did not need it; and yet he has lugged it in. My hon. friend paid a high compliment-and not too high-to the members of the Government and Legislature of Ontario. I know these men, and I believe what he said, that they are honest men; they are not bigots, but fair-minded men. These, then, it seems to me, are the men to whom he should go. He never has expressed such high confidence in the men who sit on the treasury benches in this House. And yet, desiring honestly to do a great .thing for the cause which, he says, commands his sympathy, he deliberately turns away from the men in whom he has confidence and comes to press an impossible task upon men in whom, he has expressly declared over and over again, he has no confidence.
Disallowance is no good, he says; disallowance is no good, said my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) over and over again; disallowance will not do what is desired, said others in this debate, over and over again. iHow is it-and here is a question that troubles me-that for week after week, for month after month, an agitation has been carried on, paper and ink have been freely used, and thousands upon thousands of people were led to sign a petition to this Parliament, asking for disallowance as a remedy for a grievance which is alleged? My right hon. friend, whose hand is upon the strings of the whole country, and especially upon the strings of Quebec, should have advised his friends that this was only provocation and embarrassment. But all .that time there was no word from him advising-
No, no.
-those in whom-
No, I never advised,'-because I never was consulted, iand never knew. If I had been consulted a different course would have been, taken.
My right hon. friend is about as innocent a youth for an old politician as I have met in a long time.
I will admit mo such imputation. I say here on my honour that I never heard of these petitions, I never was consulted about them. The hon. gentleman can take my word or not as he chooses.

My right hon. friend is quite wrong:	I had no intention
of suggesting doubt of his statement that he did not know these things. But the mystery deepens. How a man like my right hon. friend, who has been forty years in politics', who knows the ropes, who keeps even with the current of public thought- how all these things could have gone on and he never have heard of it surprises me. There is another thing with regard to my right hon. friend. In all his speech I did not hear a single word of condemnation for the firebrands, for the violators of law on the other side of the question, and not only the violation, ibut the denial, and and the flouting of it under iny. right hon. friend's front windows. He must have known that. Where, in Ottawa or elsewhere, did my right hon. friend say a word on behalf of the majesty of the denied law, a word as to the short-sightedness of the men who fight the'law on any such lines?
My hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham)-I must get back to him because I like him so well-I think, has got on strange ground to-night. With long years of experience, with high standing in his party-some time, it is rumoured, to be the leader of his party-what strange heresy is this he has been preaching here to-night? He has invited both sides to this dispute to evade the judgments of the courts of the land and pay no heed to them.
I have not invited them, hut I have stated facts which everybody knows.

What solid ground can we go upon if we are to follow the hon. gentleman? Up to tlhe present time I think we have had solid ground m this, that whenever legislation was enacted

 which was supposed to be wrong, gradually it went up from court to court until at last it
got to the highest tribunal, and when that highest tribunal pronounced its judgment every oitizen bowed /to that judgment. Is that not the only safety that we have in a country like this? My hon. friend to-night scouts such doctrine as that, goes to the one side, the enacting- power, and says: "If the Privy Council says you are wrong, you will evade their judgment, and you will find some way of perpetrating that [DOT]wrong again." He goes to the aggrieved party, and says: "If the judgment goes against your wishes, you will not be satisfied, and you will not bow to the law." That is not good doctrine in a country like ours, -but perhaps it is only a temporary aberration in my hon. friend.
That is all.
I know he will come back to his right mind.
Ask any lawyer, and he will tell you it is true, just the same.

I am 6orry, myself, that this resolution ever came into this House. I say that for all purposes which have been avowed by my right hon. friend and my hon. friend who has just spoken, for all purposes of making a plea, of expressing their sentiments, there was no necessity for bringing this resolution. But the resolution was brought, and just the last few words of my hon. friend gave me a clue as to why it was brought.	He has been pointing the
moral and adorning the tale. Nothing in that resolution of advice, or anything of the kind he says; but when he comes to apply it, as he did a moment or two ago, he says: "Just let the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minis,ter of Finance or one or two other members of the Government take this message from us and go down and use their influence with the Ontario Government, and they can settle it in a minute." And, if they do not happen to be able to settle it and the Ontario Government say, "We stand by what we have done," then my hon. friend would have got what he wanted-a chance to blame the Government and to trumpet it all over this country that they did not do what they might have done. That gives a pretty good indication of why this resolution was brought in.

Does the hon. gentleman really mean to say that was my motive in making that suggestion? I absolutely deny

that I had anything of the kind in my mind; I treated this question from a higher standpoint.

Then my hon.
friend is very unfortunate in making the application in the way he did, because his last argument included laying this burden of duty on certain members of the Government, and that if they would take it up and go down to Toronto the whole matter would be fixed and everybody would be satisfied.

I will go with them if
they will take me.

We would be glad of your company.
I listened to the speech that was delivered here by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) with a good deal of interest. The (position of the west was strongly put by him. I am sorry this resolution was brought, (because it makes a pathway for succeeding resolutions. Once you open the pathway to a resolution' which involves an interference with a legislature which is acknowledged by hon. gentlemen themselves to have enacted within its powers a law which they would not ask to be disallowed, the very moment you open a path with reference to the province of Ontario, you open it for every province in this wide country. I repeat what my right hon. friend the leader of this Government (Sir Robert Borden) said, that if that is to become a habit and a practice in this House, no province is safe from the reproof, the admonition and the interference of a majority in this House which may choose to interfere with its just rights of legislation. If it is possible to do that with the province of Ontario, it is possible to do it with the province of Quebec, and the province of Quebec is the last province in this Dominion which, from its own standpoint and holding to its own ideals, should have helped to brush out a path for action such as that into this Dominion Parliament, into this House of Commons-the very last. Here, with reference to the other provinces, we may be divided; but something might occur with reference to the province of Quebec on which the vast majority of the Dominion would feel one way, whilst Quebec had felt and legislated another way, and then you would have, not a resolution which can be defeated as this will be defeated in this House, but a resolution which might pass this House and

impose interference with the action of the province of Quebec.
Then, what in the wide world is the use of framing a resolution with a mandate in it unless you are determined to carry out the mandate? A mandate looks for a remedy. The remedy in this case is the amendment of the law. We pass the mandate-put it as mildly as you please, we pass it. We are no men, we have not been serious and in earnest, if, having commenced, having put our hand to the plough, we do not see the end of the furrow; and, if the Government of Ontario does not take our suggestion, then there will be a duty laid upon us to use something more than suggestion. Otherwise, it is futile to bring a resolution of that kind, and futility is the chief characteristic of this action of my right hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, the subject which is before this House is so important that, although there has been some considerable discussion of this resolution, I feel it due to myself as a member from the province of Ontario that I should not cast a silent vote upon this question. Let me say further, Sir, that I propose to give reasons, as shortly and clearly as I may, why, in my opinion this resolution is properly here, and why, in my opinion it should be supported.
The hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) who has just sat down, has found fault with the fact that this resolution is here. Why is it, he says, that a resolution of this kind should be before this House? Let me say to him that, in the first place, this House can only speak by resolutions. Let me say to him, in the second place, that we are here as representatives of the whole of the Dominion of Canada, and as such we have a right to have put before us and to have aired any grievance which any portion of the people of the Dominion of Canada may suffer; and it is for us to say then whether or not, that grievance having been put before us as representatives, not of any province but of the whole Dominion, it is fit >and' meet that we should take some action in regard to it.
The resolution that is presented to the House to-night by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Ernest Lapointe) is not without precedent, and I would give to the House a precedent established in 1872, which I take from the Journals of this House. At that time Mr. Colby, a Con-

servative membber for Stanstead, there having been some trouble with regard to a school law in the province of New Brunswick, moved:
That this House regrets that the School Act recently passed in New Brunswick is unsatisfactory to a portion of the inhabitants of that province, and hopes that it may' be so modified during the next session of the Legislature of New Brunswick as to remove any just grounds of discontent that now exist.
The question went to a vote, and in those days they were no pigmies as they are not to-day, but big 'broad-minded men, who sat in the House of Commons representing this Dominion, men who had quite as much appreciation of provincial rights as any man in this House has to-day. Amongst the men who voted for that resolution, I find, were Blake, Cartwright, Hincks, Howe, Mackenzie, Tilley, Tupper, and Sir John A. Macdonald, Could we, I ask, in all sincerity, have a better precedent than was there laid down by the very men who were responsible for the foundation and confederation of the Dominion of Canada. There you had men, who recognized that a grievance existed in a certain portion of the Dominion, who were here as representatives collectively of the whole Dominion, bringing the matter before the Legislative Council of New Brunswick, and asking, as this resolution to-night asks, with all humility and with all respect that the Legislature look into the grievance, and give at least some aid towards its removal.
Sir, there are two things in the Dominion of Canada that are uppermost to-day. One is the winning of this war, and the other is the unity of the races in the Dominion of Canada. No country can be great, no country can prosper, where there is not unity among the inhabitants. Of provincial rights, let me say this: I was brought up in the cradle of provincial rights, and my father before me. No man ever held stronger views about provincial rights than he, and those views he translated into positive and concrete action in the province of Ontario. I inherited them, and I feel as strongly in regard to them as any man could feel. But I challenge any man on the other side of the House to show me wherein provincial rights are by one jot or tittle infringed in this resolution. Further, I say that to raise the question of provincial rights in this debate is to go far afield of the question at issue. The hon. member for Kamouraska, the mover of this resolution, stated his position in language so plain that nobody could misunderstand his
meaning. He started his speech by stating that had disallowance- been moved in this House he would have been one of the first to oppose it. He further said:
Indeed, I personally believe that disallowance would have been unwise; the remedy might, perhaps, have increased the disease. Coercion of any kind will not settle the difficulties.
I am a true Liberal and a believer in provincial rights. I will go so far as to admit that to be effective and successful any final settlement of this question must be made in Ontario and by Ontario herself. But, Sir, is it not the right of this Parliament, while declining to interfere with the provincial legislation of Ontario by the exercise of the power of disallowance or otherwise, to appeal to the rulers of that province for a generous and peaceful settlement of this disturbing question and for a redress of the grievances of the minority?
I ask, could anything be more simple, and at the same time more forcible, or could anything show a greater appreciation of what the mover of the resolution conceived his position to be? Granting all the provincial rights that Ontario possesses, he said, will you not consent to make some effort towards the peaceable settlement of the grievance which we think exists. That is all he asks. It is plain, simple, direct, and is the plea of a minority to a vast majority. It puts in words a plea to which the House surely cannot fail to pay heed, so far as the passing of this resolution is concerned, a plea for some effort towards settlement of this very great difficulty.
My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce has talked about a mandate, and the right hon. the Prime Minister has talked about admonition arid direction. I defy any man who reads that resolution through to show me where the mandate is, where the admonition is, or where the direction, or even the hint of direction to the province of Ontario or to its Legislative Assembly is. The resolution reads:
That this House especially at this time of universal sacrifice and anxiety, when all energies should be concentrated on the winning of the war, would, while fully recognizing the principle of provincial rights and tne necessity of every child being given a thorough English education, respectfully suggest to the Legislative Assembly the wisdom of making it clear that the privilege of the children of French parentage of being taught in their mother tongue be not interfered with.*
A grievance there undoubtedly is. Everybody in the province of Ontario knows that fckat grievance exists. I am not saying that it is right or that it is wrong, but I do say that to pass this resolution would only do justice to those who suppose that they have a grievance. If it should be proved, after due inquiry, that
V

they had no grievance, the passing of this resolution would prejudice nobody. If that is so, then why cavil? Why not at least let us say as men, having the best interests of the country at heart, that it being a matter of common knowledge that the grievance is there, we will pass this resolution, and if we do, can we possibly, in any way whatever, or by any stretch of imagination, be said to be admonishing the Ontario Government or infringing upon provincial rights? Although no man will uphold provincial rights more strongly than I, where provincial rights are not being entrenched upon, and where a civil request is made, no demand, it would not in the least prejudice the best interests of our country, which we are supposed to be here to uphold, if we adopt this resolution. May I say to some hon. gentlemen who sit on the other side of the House, that were they to vote for the resolution as it stands, they would only be upholding the traditions of Sir John Macdonald, whose principles they profess to so greatly admire? The passing of that resolution will mean that there will be greater unity in Canada and a closer adhesion of races and peoples.
I have been told by my friends, some of them political, some of them otherwise, that, as a member for an Ontario constituency, for me to vote for the resolution means political oblivion. All I have to say is that if the time ever comes in this House why I cannot give good reasons for the faith that is in me, for the measures I support, I sincerely hope that I shall not continue to be here. I can do little less than satisfy ipy own conscience as a man, and if I do vote for the resolution, and if it does mean political oblivion, I only have to say that the passing of political parties, or the passing of any one member of a political party, makes little difference, as they are sure that they have done full and complete justice to the cause which they are supposed to have at heart, and if they pass out they do so feeling satisfied with the course which they have pursued. Ever since I have been in public life-and it is not a matter of yesterday-at periodical times, there have been raised racial and religious questions within the province of Ontario. Well do I know whereof I speak, but I want to say this, that if we here to-night, with this resolution before us, can, by the elrer-cise of a little moderation, and by setting aside all party associations, pass this resolution and bring about a stifling of these racial cries which are rending Canada from time to time, we will have done full justice

to ourselves, and we will have done a benefit to Canada as a whole and to thr provinces collectively and individually.

Mr. Speaker, it does not often happen, but when it does happen I doubt if there is anything more solemn than to hear a man delivering hie own funeral oration. There has Ibeen more solemnity in the funeral oration just delivered than there was in that of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). That hon. gentleman took a melancholy pleasure in the prospect that his attitude upon this question was going to mean his political funeral. I think he hopes to escape the funeral by getting away to some place where that funeral is not going to occur. Any person reading the resolution before the House must marvel at the character of the speeches that have been made in support of it. We heard a great deal yesterday, last night and today, about the right-the inalienable right -of the French Canadians to the use of their language in the public schools of Ontario. There is not one solitary word in the resolution about rights. The word is ''privileges". I venture to say that if the minority have enjoyed these privileges, as quoted in the resolution, in a province such as Ontario, that province surely is not open to the censure of being intolerant and that this Parliament is not in a position to advise the legislature to exercise justice and tolerance. The fact that these privileges have been enjoyed so long shows that the Government of Ontario has always been tolerant or these privileges would not have existed so long as they did as privileges.
We are asked to convey an admonition to the Ontario Government. Why? Not because there is a grievance. The resolution does not say there is a grievance. The hon. member (Mr. Pardee), who sat down just now, said that there is a grievance but the resolution does not say there is a grievance. The resolution says that some people say there is a grievance and because some people say there is a grievance we are asked to give an admonition to the Ontario Government. I know some people say there is a grievance. My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid LaurieT) must have heard of this griev-vance but why should we be asked to adjudicate upon this matter upon hearsay evidence of that sort? The hon. member (Mr. Lapointe), who introduced the subject, should have been sure that there was a grievance, he should have made the reso-

Int.ion state there was a grievance, but instead of that he simply states that some people in the province of Ontario say there is a grievance. I am not going to deal with the question at any length. This is a difficult question of long duration. As long ago as 1885 complaints were made of the bilingual schools in Ontario. In 1885 first, and in 1889 next, the Government of Sir Oliver Mowat, who was praised yesterday by the leader of the Opposition as a man of great breadth of view and toleration, had to take the matter in hand through his Minister of Education, Sir Geo. W. Ross. No man questioned the toleration of these men. The question had to come before them and it did come before them. It was brought up in the House and an attempt-a rather feeble attempt indeed-was made to remedy it. The condition of these schools became worse instead of better.
When the present Government of Ontario came into power these conditions had to be met. Representations were made. It was not that the Protestants were suffering to any great extent. As a matter of fact it was Bishop Fallon who complained that efficient education was not 'being given in these English-French schools in his diocese of Essex. A commissioner, Dr. Merchant, was appointed. No man will say that he was a man of intolerant views. He examined into these schools, and his report bore out the contention of His Lordship Bishop Fallon. And the conditions were met. I was glad to hear my hon. friend from South Renfrew pay so high a tribute to two or three members of the Ontatrio Government. He might have added that at that time there was at the head of the Ontario Government Sir James Whitney, a man whom French Canadians have certainly no right to regard as intolerant. No man had a finer regard for French Canadian character than Sir James Whitney. It was under him that French Canadians in Ontario received representation in the Ontario Cabinet, with full ministerial powers. That did not argue that Sir James Whitney was an intolerant man by any means. And it was while the French enjoyed this privilege of having a representative in the Government of Ontario that Regulation 17 was passed, in June, 1912. At that time Sir James was Premier, and Hon. Dr. Reaume was his Minister of Public Works, acting also in an advisory capacity with Sir James. I hope, therefore, that no one will allege that this Regulation was passed with any idea of being intolerant in any degree whatever.
My right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition expressed regret that this Government had not appealed to the province of Ontario to remedy this legislation. Similar legislation is in effect in Manitoba. My right hon. friend has considerable influence with the leader of the Government there. It is a Liberal Government and friendly to himself politically. I should like lo know whether he has used his good offices with Premier Norris of Manitoba to prevent the French-Canadians of Manitoba being placed under worse disabilities, ae. they call them, than the French in Ontario. If he has not done this in Manitoba why does he regret that this Government have not used their good offices with the Government of Ontario? I do not believe there is one solitary government in the Dominion of Canada, outside of that of the province of Quebec, that would pass such legislation and regulations as the Government of Ontario have passed with respect to the teaching in bilingual schools. I should like my right hon. friend to use his influence in having similar legislation oassed in Alberta or Saskatchewan. I know the answer he would get from Saskatchewan and other provinces in this country, where he has more influence perhaps than in Ontario. I say it does not lie in the mouth of any hon. gentleman opposite to charge the Ontario Government with being intolerant in any degree whatever. If we liked to make an appeal against certain legislation passed by the Government of Quebec this session I do not think the Speaker could rule us out of order. We should have a mighty good precedent anyway. Reference has already been made to that Act of the Government of Quebec, by which the School Boards in the province of Quebec were allowed to contribute up to five per cent of their taxes towards opposing educational legislation in the province of Ontario. The legislation could properly be disallowed by this Government. And yet I have no intention in the world of asking to have that done. I do not care what the province of Quebec does with their money. They collect it, and they can spend it amongst newspapers and lawyers, fighting this legislation, if they like. I am not going to object to that at all. At the very time that legislation was being passed in Quebec, a Quebec minister, the Minister of Justice, was passing through this House legislation the object of which was to make it a crime for any man in one province to assist in the violation of the law of any

other province. While we were passing that, the Government of Quebec were passing legislation allowing funds to fee raised for the violation of the legislation of Ontario; for that legislation can have no [DOT] other meaning.
My right hon. friend has great admiration for his people, and I do not blame him for it; it is very creditable to him. He wants to see this thing righted. He brought in this resolution, or the hon. member for Kamouraska did, as a motion of want of confidence in this Government, and then he asked the people behind him to vote as they pleased. Is he doing his full duty by the French Canadians of Ontario when he does that sort of thing? Why does he not command his whole force on the other side of the House to vote for the resolution? He could, if he. would. I never saw the time yet when his will was not law with his followers on that side of the House. They always vote, at his command. They "live in his mild, magnificent eye." There is nothing that he can ask that they would not do. If he demands their support for this resolution he will! get it. And if he is sincere in trying to have this resolution passed and remedial legislation enacted, for the benefit of his compatriots in Ontario, he will .command the full support of uis followers on that side of the House.
My hon. friend the member from Nioolet (Mr. Lamarche) has declared that this law is ultra vires. I think it is too late to do that now. He should have told it to the courts before they declared that it was not ultra vires. It was up to him to do it. With his superior judgment one would have thought he had foresight enough to offer his opinion to the court before judgment was delivered.
It is too late to-night for me to speak at any great length, and I am not going to do it. I hope I shall not be accused of having any grudge against the French language, because I have not. I like the French language. Its music, its melody, its poetry and its rhythm appeal to me. But I like it as a language. I do not accept it as a fetish, or revere it as a religion, as my hon. friends from Kamouraska and Wright apparently do. French is a language that all of us on both sides of the House ought to know, no matter what our nationality. Hut I will say this, that hon. gentlemen who attempt to make capital against the Government of the province of Ontario by alleging that the French Canadian people nave grievances in that province, are not 
doing themselves any good and are stirring up strife which they will find it very hard (to subdue later on.

Mr. *Speaker, I wish to eay a few words on this question, and, as the hour is getting late, I will be very brief. I do not purpose discussing constitutional rights; I will take (the broad ground taken yesterday by my right hon. leader, .that by the law of nations the French race-call it a conquered race if you like; I prefer to say that this country was ceded by France to England -had the right to keep its language. When the question was discussed in 1890 on a motion to abolish the French language in the legislature of the Northwest Territories, an eminent lawyer, a man who later became Minister of Justice and afterwards a judge of the (Supreme Court of (Canada, Hon. (David Mills, said that he thought it was not necessary for Chevalier de Levi6 to stipulate in the articles of capitulation *anything with regard to the French language; that when their usages and civil *and religious liberty were accorded to the French people, that meant also their language, because those usages and that civil *and religious liberty were . preserved in that language.
In regard to the question of the teaching of French in this province, the French language was taught many years before *Confederation, and, although the Confederation Act does not expressly stipulate that the French language has. a legal status in Ontario, still section 133 states that *French is an official language in the country, and, that being the case, it should *certainly have a right to be taught to the citizens of that province. That was the interpretation held by the 'Council of Public Instruction before 1867. As my hon. friend from Wright (Mr. Devlin) mentioned yesterday, the followihg letter was written on the 24th of April, 1857, by the Superintendent of Education, Dr. Ryerson, to the trustees of a school section in the township of Charlottenburg in the county of *Glengarry:
Gentlemen:
I have the honour to state in reply to your letter of the 16th instant that, as the French is the recognized language of the country, as well as the English, it is quite proper and lawful for the trustees to allow both languages to be taught in their schools to children whose parents may desire them to learn both.
My hon. friend the Postmaster General (Mr. Casgram) read last night a resolution adopted hy tbo Legislature of Upper Can-

ada in 1792 ordering that the records of the legislature and the statutes of the province should be published in French as well as in English. The French' language has always been taught in the schools of the province, public and separate.
My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) this afternoon said that Regulation 17 gave a concession to the French people of Ontario, that it was not a restriction. I differ from him in regard to that. Before Regulation 17 was promulgated full scope was given to the teaching of French in the separate schools of the province. There is nothing in the Separate School Act limiting the teaching of French. In the Public Schools Act there is a section which says that the teaching must be in the English language unless the pupil cannot understand that language, in which case the teacher can impart instruction in the mother tongue of the pupil. Regulation 17, however, applies both to public and separate schools, and it applies more to separate schools in practice, because all the schools that were classified in 1912 as English-French schools were separate schools, which were inspected before 1912 by a French Canadian inspector. The list of schools which was made in 1912 for the inspectors was never enlarged, and there is no public school included in that list. Therefore Regulation 17 limits the teaching of French in the separate schools of Ontario, whereas, before the promulgation of that regulation, there was no limitation and the teacher could impart all the instruction necessary in the mother tongue of the pupil.
My hon. friend from Kingston (Mr.Nickle) last night put a wrong interpretation upon paragraph 4 of Regulation 17. He contended that the word " hitherto " did not imply that French could not be taught in a school established since 1912. To appreciate Regulation 17, we must see how it operates, and I can give two cases of schools established in my county since 1912 which are not attended by any English-speaking pupils, and still the Department of Education will not recognize them as schools where French can be taught, because, they are not schools where French was a subject of study before 1912 when Regulation 17 was promulgated. The trustees of those schools appoint teachers who impart instruction in French, but as those schools are considered to be outside the law, they do not receive the legislative grants nor the grants from the county council.
My hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) this afternoon tried to create the impression that the Government was bonus-ing the English-French schools of Ontario. Instead of bonusing them, the Government is starving them, becauses, since 1912, some of the English-French schools of Ontario have not received any grants from the Government nor any grants from the county council, because the latter grants are paid on the reports of the inspectors; and, the inspectors not reporting, the county treasurer has no authority to pay the grants collected by the county council. It is true that the last paragraph of Regulation 17 permits the Government to make a special grant to a school on the report of all the inspectors approved by the chief inspector. (Reading):
An English-French school, which is unable to provide the salary necessary to secure a teacher with the aforesaid qualifications, shall receive a special grant in order to assis* 'n doing so.
I do not, however, know of a case since 1912 where such a grant has been made by the department. When this regulation was promulgated, the Government appointed two sets of inspectors, English-speaking inspectors and French-speaking inspectors. There was no necessity for this. Before 1912 the bilingual schools were inspected by bilingual inspectors, but when this regulation was made inspectors were appointed, as I have stated, and precedence was given to the English-speaking inspectors. I say that the French-speaking inspectors were better qualified to visit these schools because they knew English as well as French. When the Government made all inspectors equal in 1913 they gave control to the chief inspector of the province. For a teacher to teach French outside of the first course he must have the approval of the chief inspector. This puts the English-French schools under the control of the chief inspector, and he is the only person who can say, outside the first grade, whether there should be one hour or one minute devoted to French teaching in the schools. I will not go into the question whether it is preferable to teach the child in its mother tongue or not-that has been very well discussed by my right hon. leader and others. But perhaps I might give my own experience. My family moved to Ontario when I was six years of age. When I began to go to school the only school available was one entirely English. I learned to read English, but I did not know the value of the words. A

I will not go over the whole matter. I will only say that they reported to the department in 1913 that Regulation 17 was taken to mean that French could not be used as the language of communication and that it was regarded as an attempt to gradually eliminate the French language from the schools. So you see Mr. Speaker, it was not clear, and is not clear yet, and it is very important that it should be made clear. I was sorry to see that while some hon. gentlemen opposite, the Postmaster General for example, ex-presed the opinion that Regulation 17 was unfair, they declined to help us to remonstrate or to induce the Government of Ontario to afford a remedy to the grievances of the minority.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Jus-tict):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not propose to detain the House at this late hour for more than a few moments, but there are one or two things I would like to say before registering my vote upon this resolution.
In the first place, in passing, I would make one observation with regard to some of the things that have been said by the hon. member for Nicolet (Mr. Lamarche) in connection with the report addressed to His Royal Highness upon the question of disallowance. I noted that the hon. gentleman premised his observations by saying that he had not carefully read the report. He might have dispensed with the explanation, for when he proceeded it became quite self-evident that he had not done so. He was pleased to criticise some of the reasons advanced in support of the conclusion which was reached. He admitted that he did not think that disallowance would have been of any use, and then in a somewhat extraordinary consequence he said that if he had the responsibility he would have advised disallowance. I think that in face of the numerous opinions which have been expressed upon that question I may safely leave the reasons in that report to the judgment of people who may consider the matter of sufficient importance to carefully read the report before proceeding to discuss it.
Upon the question of the resolution, as it is before the House, we have certainly had an interesting debate. I have listened to the greater part of it with great interest.
I have learned a great deal; perhaps I may be among these whom the right hon. gentleman who leads the Opposition thought would be better and wiser men 
by reason of this discussion.
1 a.m. I want to point out the one question upon which it seems to me we are called upon to vote, and the one question upon which I desire to make it perfectly clear that I express an opinion by my vote. That is the question of the propriety of this House sitting in judgment upon the Legislative Assembly of the province of Ontario, or of any other province, and proceeding, as has been pointed out so forcibly by my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce, to try that Legislative (Assembly and find it guilty without it being heard or had opportunity of being heard of action that has been described in terms of varying degrees of strength. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat described it as a crime. The hon. member for Nicolet said that this was the opportunity to make the injustice which the Legislative Assembly of Ontario had perpetrated ring from one ocean to the other. This House is asked to solemnly pronounce that that injustice has been proved, as has been pointed out, without the slightest opportunity of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario, the elected representatives of the people of Ontario, elected with an express mandate to deal with' subjects of this kind, having had the slightest opportunity to be heard. The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) justified the bringing of this matter before this House on the ground that this House is the high court before which it was proper that all grievances Should be tried out, and we are asked in our capacity as members of that high court of Parliament to pronounce that the Legislative Assembly of Ontario had been guilty of grave injustice, though th'ey had not had an opportunity to [DOT]be heard. I can conceive of nothing more fundamentally unjust than the condemnation of a man, or of a body of men, who [DOT]have not been heard and who have had no opportunity of being heard, and the clearest demonstration that we are stepping beyond any attribute that belongs to us, when, we undertake to pronounce that judgment, is to be found in the fact that there is no possible method by which we could have that [DOT]alleged culprit before us to say one word on his own behalf.
We have had the Legislative Assembly of [DOT]Ontario on trial before this House for two days, and the Legislative Assembly has not been represented here and has not been heard, and yet we are asked to pronounce the judgment I have mentioned. The right

bon. gentleman who leads the Opposition says:	Oh, this is a very harmless thing;
this is the mildest of suggestions," and, when honourable gentlemen come to support their motion that this House make this mildest of suggestions, they find it necessary to produce proof of this alleged injustice, of this alleged wrongdoing on the part of the Legis-alleged wrongdoing on the part of the Legislative Assembly of Ontario. Unless we are prepared to say that they have established it, there is absolutely no basis for us going to the Legislature of Ontario with the suggestion. I must do the justice to the hon. member for West Lamtoton (Mr. Pardee) of saying that he at least tried to avoid the grave responsibility of pronouncing that serious verdict against a party unheard, but in order to do so he found himself reduced to say:	"I do not know
whether they are right; I do not know whether they are wrong; but we will pass this resolution, and when we have passed it we will go to Toronto and see whether, upon the inquiry we will make, there was any occasion for us to pass it." That is putting this high court of Parliament in a dignified position indeed. I have been elected a member of this Parliament to represent those who send me here and to take my share in the legislation and the administration of those matters that are confided to this Parliament, and therefore I cannot help asking myself what mandate I have to determine, according to my views, what is the proper system of education for the province of Ontario or what the representatives of the people of Ontario, elected with an express mandate, should declare to be the proper system of education for that province.
Would my hon. friend be prepared to vote upon a resolution in this House in favour of Home Rule?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
thinks he has struck me on a tender spot; but I would point out to the hon. gentleman that relations between this Parliament and His Majesty the King are somewhat different from the relationship between this Parliament and any of the legislatures of this country. When a Home Rule resolution was passed and this House decided to make a humble address to His Majesty the King, it put before him that in the judgment of this House it was a matter of interest to the Empire as a whole and every one of the Dominions, including Canada, that that particular matter should be taken
up and considered. We were really dealing with a question that in a manner affects this entire Empire, but to suggest that there is anything analogous between our then going to His Majesty the King and putting before him that every portion of the Empire was interested in seeing the British constitution given practical effect to throughout the entire Empire, and this Parliament, occupying the position it does, addressing the legislature of the provinces, this Parliament being the creature of the same statute that created those legislatures, and this Parliament having allotted to it an exclusive field of legislation, and they having allotted to them, in the most express terms, another exclusive field, is something that is absolutely without foundation. If the hon, member wants to iput me on the horns of a dilemma he will have to ask me another question.
Before deciding not todisallow this Act, did the Minister not have before him the answer of the Ontario Government on this question?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Most assuredly I did.
The Government therefore has been heard?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: His Royal Highness in Council heard the Government of Ontario, and hon. gentlemen do not complain of what His Royal Highness in Council did after having heard the Government of Ontario. But they come to this Parliament,, that did not hear the Government of Ontario, and they ask Parliament to take-action. I think this hon. gentleman also-will have to find some other question before I get very much embarrassed.
I understood the minister to say that the Legislative Assembly of Ontario had been put upon trial without, having been heard.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In this House most assuredly the Legislative Assembly of Ontario has been put on trial for two days and there has been no opportunity of it being heard, and in the very nature of things it would not be possible to give it that opportunity. And I believe that is a conclusive demonstration of the fact that this high court of Parliament is proceeding to act in a manner that is fundamentally opposed to the most simple rules applicable to any British court of justice.
Now perhaps I shall be permitted to go-back to the subject I was endeavouring to

abbreviate as much as I could when I was interrupted. I asked myself what mandate I had to express my views a3 regards the best system of education for any province, or in that connection jpy views in regard to the jealous care which should be given to the respect of every right, or every believed right-I am prepared to go so far as to say of every prejudice-that can be reasonably considered without injury to the common weal, of every minority. I am free to say that as a general principle I am not here to judge whether it is complied with in one place or in another place; but I am quite prepared to say that in my judgment there is nothing more sacred than the right of the minority within a democracy unless it be the sacred trust reposed in the majority to see that the right of the minority is preserved. I am not here to apply any principles of that kind although they are principles that I think would meet with general assent. I am not here to apply them in particular cases. There is no case before this Parliament that this Parliament has, properly speaking, any right to pass upon or adjudicate upon. Nor is there any room for us to determine to what extent these principles have been applied, or have failed to be applied in a particular province. But ;we are asked to take this step in the interest of a minority which is represented as having a grievance. There is no doubt that any possible grievance of any minority is a most important thing. I have always been, I suppose I always shall be, within this country one of the minority. In my [DOT]own province I am one of the minority from the point of view of language. Throughout this Dominion I am one of the minority from the point of view of religion. Since I have mentioned the fact that I am one of the minority in my own province, I might, perhaps, ibe permitted to digress one moment just to say that as one. of the minority I am proud of my own province, in that I .am able to affirm that one does not feel in the province of Quebec that he is subjected to injustice or inconveniences by reason of being in the minority in regard to the recognition of every right to which he is entitled. I say that of course without suggesting that the same is not the case everywhere. I have no case and this House has no case before it to judge.

On that occasion it was my privilege to hear the famous speech, which is still ringing in my ears, which was delivered by the leader of the Opposition, and which proved to be the last nail in the coffin of the Manitoba School Remedial Bill, which waL. brought into the House by the Tory Administration of the time. Twenty years have passed over the head of the leader of the Opposition, and I am pleased to say that the speech he made yesterday was just as eloquent as the one he delivered twenty years ago. He received just as much support, he was cheered just as much by his supporters from the province of Quebec yesterday as he was at that time. But while my mind dwelt on the tragedy which took place in 1826, and the comedy now being enacted in this House, I could not help thinking that his eloquence at that time served to kill a practical and constitutional measure that would have brought relief to his compatriots in Manitoba, while to-day that eloquence is used for no other purpose than to create political strife- in this country. But no doubt to-morrow he will be hailed as a hero in that section of the press that has covered him with obliquy and poured the grossest abuse upon him for the last few years, while I and my colleagues, who refuse to be trapped by this political trickery, will be branded as traitors to our race, as traitors to our creed, as traitors to our religion, perhaps as traitors to our own children. But history will record-and history, I submit, is the final judge, and my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition will not and cannot escape that judgment-history will record that twenty years ago, when he could have helped his compatriots he refused to do so. And to-day he is not taking the course that is- the best calculated to help the minority in Ontario. I do not wish to say more. I refuse to support the present motion, not because I am not in sympathy with the sentiments expressed therein. I regret that my compatriots in Ontario have a serious grievance, and I hope and trust that the great province of Ontario will adopt every means in its power to redress that grievance. I shall vote against this motion because it is unconstitutional, and 
is introduced in such a way and at such a time that it can effect no good purpose, and may perhaps do mortal harm to the cause I have at heart.

As I
heard the observations of the. hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat I could not but wonder what the verdict of history would be on this Parliament, sitting here at half past two o'clock in the morning to consider a resolution that can result in no action by this Parliament, sitting upon a futile resolution at a time when thousands of our fellow-countrymen are at this very moment, offering their lives upon the plains of France and Flanders in defence of this free Parliament. I wonder if it has dawned upon the minds of the men responsible for the introduction of this resolution that the very existence of our institutions is at stake, and that the question for which our fellow Canadians are dying to-night is whether this shall continue to be a British country, or, as the hon. member for Sbefford (Mr. Boivin) has said, a German colony. That seems to me to be the question that we should consider, and I cannot but think that history will weigh very carefully, and deter= mine very accurately, the position of the gentlemen responsible for the introduction into this Parliament at this time of a question that divides race against Tace, that makes for dissension and not for unity, and that would in the end destroy the Confederation, instead of carrying forward the work of the founders that made possible this Dominion. For the question involved is simply a constitutional one in the first instance. When I think of the labours of the Fathers of Confederation that made possible the uniting of the old provinces' and the creation of this Confederation, I realize that that was done by a system of compromise in which each gave up a little of his rights in order that there should he a united Confederation'. The rights of minorities and the privileges of majorities have been determined by a statute called the British North America Act, which is the constitution of this eoun- ' try, and that constitution allocated to the several provinces and the Dominion the powers they should possess and the legislative jurisdiction they should exercise. It was determined.-and it seems to me very properly-that the power with relation, to education should be exercised by the provinces, subject only to the exercise by this

Parliament of that jurisdiction which may become necessary for the .purpose of giving remedial legislation to minorities, Protestant or Catholic, that may be affected. The observations that have just been made by the hon. member for Montrmagny (Mr. l'Esiperance) Tecall the fact that in days gone by this Parliament was prevented from taking the only legislative action that could ibe taken by it under one of the sections of the constitution to remedy wrongs that had been done to minorities in relation to education. The same forces that twenty years ago prevented these remedies from being granted, that in days gone by called -out ".Hands off Manitoba," are to-day the forces that are crying aloud to the people of this Canada of ours, east, west, north and south, " Hands on Ontario." If it was right that twenty years ago the province of Manitoba should be left to work out its . own destiny, and make its own legislation in regard to education, how much1 more is it right to-day, in the light of twenty years' more experience, that each province should be permitted to work out its own salvation with relation to education of the children within its boundaries.
My hon. friend has referred to a precedent that would indicate that possibly this Parliament in days gone by had interfered with the free exercise of power by the provinces. I was surprised, I was astounded, when the hon. member for Lambton (Mr. Pardee) so dared in this free Parliament to inaccurately discuss what took place in it in 1872. If he were not a member of the legal profession and did not understand the language he read, I might not feel so much called upon to say that if he had turned back the page he read from he would have found that every observation and every statement he made to this House on that point was calculated to leave a false impression. I should like him to understand that when a man reads to this House a precedent dating back to 1872, indicating action taken by this Parliament with reference to a matter of this kind, then at least he should read the whole record, and not mangle it. And it ill became a member of the legal profession, with his long parliamentary experience, not to have communicated to the House that the motion before it at that time was a motion moved by Mr. Costigam for the disallowance of the New Brunswick School Act. That was the question that this Parliament was asked to consider. Had he turned
back he would have found on page 134 of the Journals of the House for 1872, that Mr. Costigan, on the 20th of May, made a motion, seconded by Mr. Renaud, directing the attention of His Excellency the Governor General to certain allegations regarding the New Brunswick School Act, and calling upon him at the earliest possible period to disallow the said New Brunswick School law. That was a proper subject to bring before this Parliament and for this Parliament to consider. It was within the constitutional rights of any member of the House to ask that a motion should be submitted for the disallowance of the measure. After the debate had proceeded, it was moved in amendment by Mr. Graham, seconded by Mr. Bolton, that the Constitution itself should be amended (Journals of the House, 1872\ page 155). Later on, another amendment was submitted, and finally (Journals, 1872, p. 177) the amendment to which reference has been made by my hon. friend from Lambton was submitted, not as a substantive motion, not as a motion asking the House to take direct action, but as an amendment to a motion asking for the disallowance of the statute as a way out, that matter having been properly before the House.

That this House regrets that the School Act, recently passed in New Brunswick is unsatisfactory to a portion of the inhabitants of that province and hopes that it may be so modified during the next session of the legislature of New Brunswick as to remove any ground of discontent that now exists.
