That motion was stronger than this one.

It was not only not stronger than this one, but it was not in

the same terms, because the motion submitted. asked for an interference with the right to exercise its power on the part of the Legislature of New Brunswick, and the Parliament of Canada, guided alike by the genius of Cartier and Macdonald, and the logic of Dorion and the gentlemen surrounding him, and the great Blake and Tilley and Tupper, said: " Hands off New Brunswick; let New Brunswick work out her own salvation in fear and trembling as best she may, having regard alike to the rights of minorities and the privileges of majorities."

Does my hon. friend pretend that Parliament could not have voted down the motion for disallowance without being obliged to adopt the amendment to send a request to the Government and Legislature of New Brunswick to remedy the matter?

I am not pretending anything. If my hon. friend wants to look for pretence, he will find it with the gentlemen who are moving this resolution. If he wants to look for it, he need not look far either to the, right or to the left. So far as that question is concerned, it was not competent, in view of the amendments that had been submitted, for that motion to be voted on at that time, because it was realized by Sir John Abbott, then Mt. Abbott, that the amendments that were submitted involved a change in the British North America Act which, as was pointed out, meant an amendment to the constitution which, as was further pointed out, could not be made by that Parliament, and so Mr. Colby, not in amendment to the proposed motion, but in amendment to the proposed amendment, moved:
That the matter be referred to the law officers of the British Crown and submitted to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council for determining the rights and powers alike of the Parliament of Canada and of the legislature of New Brunswck.
The point to be decided was a novel point. If there be any doubt about that, let me read the words of that great statesman, the Hon. Edward Blake, who said, as reported at page 904 of the Hansard of that date:
Mr. Blake had considered from time to time since the early discussion of the subject the very difficult question of the proper interpretation of ' the Act with reference to the state of the law existing in New Brunswick on the subject of schools and he was quite free to confess that upon that subject his opinion had fluctuated, and any opinion he might then give would be given with much doubt and reservation. There was much to support in the argument put forth

by the Minister of Justice in his minute of Council. It was a conclusion at which the hon. gentleman might well have arrived and might possibly be a correct one; but he would point out a few circumstances in connection with the Act which would lead to a different conclusion. He quoted from the British North America and School Acts of New Brunswick and endeavoured to show that, although the system of denominational schools was actually established by law, still denominational teaching in the public schools was practically acknowledged, and deeply regretted the course pursued by the legislature of New Brunswick in inserting in the new School Act a clause providing that every school under that Act shall be non-sectarian.
He then proceeded to point out that'the question was properly before the Canadian Parliament to determine what might be the righ'te of that Parliament to deal with remedial legislation, which is an altogether different matter from that now before the House, on the one hand and the rights of the province of New Brunswick to amend its laws on the other. He proceeds further:
In his opinion it was in that spirit alone that the question could be successfully dealt with; but they had been asked to go a great deal further, and he felt-having been one who, upon former occasions, took an humble part in endeavouring to maintain the integrity of the constitution-bound to say a few words upon that subject. It was one thing for the provincial or the Canadian legislature to pass Act of Parliament beyond its constitutional powers, ar, action deserving of the highest reprobation, but it was quite another thing for a provincial or a general parliament to propose an amendment to the constitution.
And. then he proceeds:
But the rights and interests of the provinces would not be worth the paper on which the constitution was written if it could be said that all rights could, as a matter of course, be altered or changed on addresses alone. The Imperial Government would never take away the rights of the provincial legislature at the instance of the Dominion Parliament alone, and no more dangerous error could be fallen into. The proper mode would be not to ask Her Majesty's Government to "lake action, but to ask the local Governments to take action.
Hear, hear.

Why do hon, gentlemen say " hear, hear " to this when the resolution now proposed violates every principle of constitutional law? The only method by which the constitution of this country could be amended in regard to the rights of provinces would be by a constitutional convention at which all the provinces would unite in asking either for the enlargement or for the curtailment of their powers, and a joint address of this Parliament based upon no such constitutional convention, as Mr. Blake pointed out, would not be heeded

nor obeyed by the Imperial Pajrliament because the rights that have accrued, the .privileges that have been enjoyed and the [DOT]customs that have grown up under the constitution cannot be taken away merely because this Parliament asks them to be *taken away; they can be taken away only by a constitutional convention properly convened for the purpose of considering amendments, which convention would represent the common judgment alike of the representatives of all the provinces, and hon. gentlemen know that that must be so. Mr. Blake says further:
If any constitutional rights were infringed, Parliament had power, under the fourth clause of the Brltiesh North America Act, to interfere, and he quoted the provision giving Parliament the right to make remedial laws when necessary.
The question was properly before Parliament. It was a question involving whether or not there should be an exercise by Parliament of its remedial rights under .the constitution, the powers that iwere asserted in the Manitoba School Act in 1890, the powers that were given by which this Parliament, not clothed with original jurisdiction with regard to education, could exercise its powers under the British North America Act for the purpose of remedying wrongs that might have been done (to Iminorities, whether they be Protestant or Catholic, and it was because of that provision in. the constitution that Mr. Blake pointed out the necessity not of disallowance-he said no, do not disallow; do not refer back to the provincial legislatures alone, but get the opinion of the law officers of the Crown and of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council to the end that it may 'be determined whether or not a wrong has been done to which the remedial sections of the Act extend. That is what he asked. I will not trouble the House to-night by reading further from the debate the language used by Mr. Dorion, by Mr. afterwards Sir Albert Smith, a very great lawyer from the province of New Brunswick, who said at that time: "The cry must be: Hands off New Brunswick." This is what Mr. Smith said:
This Parliament might have the power to whip that of New-Brunswick into submission, but New-Brunswick in that event would await her opportunity to avenge the wrong.
Those are the .words of a great Liberal statesman. I turn to the words of Col. Gray, who afterwards was one of the Judges
of the Supreme Court of British Columbia who pointed out what the issue would be. I turn to the words of Mr. Dorion, who pointed out exactly what the difficulties would be and the course that shcmld be pursued. I point out Sir John Macdonald's words with relation to it. I have not time to read them all. But the consensus of opinion was that so far as this Parliament was concerned, it refused to disallow or to intervene, but sent back the Bill that was alleged to have taken away from Catholics their rights, leaving it to the legislature to determine the matter, but first determining by reference to the courts the respective and relative rights and powers, alike of the Parliament of Canada and of the Legislature of New Brunswick.
Now, let me point out what has been done in this case with reference to Ontario. I am not here to argue as to the rights and wrongs of a regulation with regard to education passed by a provincial legislature. The Privy Council has declared that the Legislature of Ontario dealing with a matter within its proper scope, has power as full and plenary as the Imperial Parliament itself may exercise with relation to the same subject matter. That legislature having exercised these powers by passing a statute defining the terms under which English and French shall be taught in their schools, this Parliament has no more power to curtail or enlarge those rights than it would have to declare whether there should be three or four minarets upon a mosque at Constantinople. Let it not be forgotten for a moment by my hon. friend from Shefford (Mr. Boivin) and my hon. friend from Nicolet (Mr. Lamarche) and those other gentlemen who have spoken here, that this very regulation and the powers under which it has been passed are now on their way to the Privy Council for judicial interpretation. The matter is sub judice. The very demand made by Mr. Blake which was acted upon by the Government of Sir John A. Macdonald, that the matter should be sent to the" courts, is (he very remedy which has been sought by hon. gentlemen opposite with relation to this legislation at this present time. Then, ii that be the case, why is it here? Are we here to revise the unuttered judgments of the Privy Council? Are we here to decide what the Privy Council shall say? If we seek a legal remedy in this case, why not leave it to the courts?
Why pass resolutions of regret, the matter is on its way to the foot of the

throne? Since when has it been the settled policy of Parliament to interfere'with suits that are being heard? Who cares for the courts? asked the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). He declares in terms that the work of the courts is to be revised alike by the majority and by the minority. The courts that we have been taught to respect and honour from our youth, as has been pointed out by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, aje not to be thought of so long as you can get a resolution into Parliament and bring about any action you will. Since when was that a doctrine of the Liberal party? Since when was disregard of constituted authority made the basis of legislative action? It is new doctrine to me that in this twentieth century and in this British country disregard of constituted authority, marchings upon the street, the flying of banners, the defiance of law, shall form the basis of action by the Parliament of Canada? I was appalled when I heard that doctrine asserted in this House. For me, trained in the law -a little-I can only say this; that if that doctrine is to prevail, then to wreck goes every opinion I have as to the security of property and the safety of the rights of individuals in this country. If you can resort to Parliament while a suit is still in progress to determine the constitutionality of a law; if you can pass a resolution in this House to determine whether a statute is ultra vires or intra vires; if you can go to the Privy Council with a resolution of this House to urge upon them in order to influence their judgment, if that is the opinion of gentlemen opposite I say that the sooner that opinion is got rid of the better. I would ask the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who is taking voluminous notes, if, when he was engaged in the steel case, or in the Dominion Coal and Iron case, he would have thought it right for the Legislature of the province of Nova Scotia to meet in solemn session and declare what should be done. At least, such action would have been within the rights of that body-that is the difference between that case and this. Property and civil rights lie within the powers of the Legislature of Nova Scotia but property and civil rights are not within our powers, and neither is education. But, in the midst of a war, it is sought to wring from the House a resolution dealing with a case that is sub judice; a cate in which a legal decision has been sought is to be prejudiced by thi6 
Parliament. Since when did all the members of this Parliament become trained jurists? Since when did they weigh finely the constitutional points involved? The hon. member for S'befford (Mr. Boivin) asserte the beautiful doctrine that when two lawyers from Quebec differ About the interpretation of an Ontario statute this Parliament should intervene. Somebody (else urges another doctrine, and others still different doctrines. But constituted authority, the courts of this country, are the tribunals to which we must appeal alike for the preservation of our rights and the declaration of their limitations. No worse doctrine can be taught than that in a democracy you can appeal to the Parliament of Canada to contravene and destroy the value of judicial decisions, especially when an appeal to the highest court is under way. I resent it. And the people iwill resent it. They may not care so *much, many of them, whether this or that fine point is at issue; but they will care if this Parliament is asked to declare for a principle that is destructive of security alike for property and of individuals, and one which this Parliament should not for a moment tolerate.

That this House, especially at this time ol universal sacrifice and anxiety, when all energy should be concentrated on the winning of the war, would, by fully recognizing the principle of provincial rights and the necessity-

-respectfully suggest to the Legislative Assembly the wisdom of making it clear that the privilege of the children of French parentage of being taught in their mother tongue be not interfered with.

gentleman will some time speak in French.

But what I ask the House is, how is it possible for this child to have a thorough knowledge of English while there is no interference with his being taught in French? Since when did this Parliament undertake to say how long French or English should be taught in the schools of any province? I challenge any constitutional lawyer on the other side to say that this Parliament has the right to say that three hours shall be given to French in Ontario and only two hours in Alberta, or has the right to say how long shall be given to English in Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, or Ontario. Then it gets down to this, that the Legislature of the province of Ontario, and that Legislature alone, has the right to decide and determine what time shall be allotted to the teaching of French, and what time shall be allotted to the teaching of English; and, if that be so which is admitted in the terms of .this resolution itself, as explained by the hon. member for Bonaventure (IMr IMarcil), with the applause of the right hon. leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) what right has this resolution in this Parliament? What right has it here at all? Has it any? If, then, you say it must be left to the province of Ontario to determine how many hours must be given to French and how many to English, in order that the child may have a thorough knowledge of English and at the same time his French education may not be interfered with, I ask this House why this resolution is here at all under those circumstances? There is only one reason, and that is a reason which, in the midst of war, one hesitates to mention, and will not mention.
Sir, I am not concerned, then, as to how Ontario exercises her legislative jurisdiction; I am not concerned how, under the constitution, New Brunswick exercises her powers. I come from the West, and I, like the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), am vitally interested in this great question that, while it affects the well-being of the East, affects even more the potential happiness and greatness of a nation yet unborn; for, from the lakes to the Rockies, there will grow up a race of men that will either be divided into the nationalities they represent, or will be taught that the language of communication, of commerce, of business, is English. They must be taught national efficiency, to adopt the words of a friend of mine who sits apposite. National efficiency in this case means that there must be taught, as the language of communication and instruction, in that great undeveloped land between the lakes and the Rockies, the language that we call English. That is all that we demand. The population of French nationality in the province of Saskatchewan is small to-day; but there are 100,000 Austrians and Germans there, meeting together to-day, yesterday, last week, and demanding the right to have their schools taught in German- why? Because of the agitation that is being carried on about bilingualism down here. That is the reason. I happened to visit Regina last year to attend court, and I saw, in a newspaper there, a letter written by the .Catholic trustees of a separate school district, resigning their trust and their office, two English-speaking Roman Catho-lios, because they said they could not longer remain upon a board that bad been dominated by the Germans of that community, in which the language of communication and instruction was sought to be made German. That was the outcome of this agitation. Let that responsibility rest where it belongs, with the men who are trying to interfere with the educational powers of the province of Ontario in this Parliament. If you say to the new settlers who come to us from Austria, Germany, Russia, Sweden, Norway, .from every nation of the world, that they are to grow each group to a little nationality of their own, with' their schools and t'heir languages, their customs, where is your Canada? .Where is your Canada? It would be like the Balkan states. Shall this be a state of little nationalities, or shall it be a great union of a great people, with one language, so far as communication .and instruction is concerned, subject to the rights guaranteed to the people of Quebec under the con-

stitution, or shall there grow up here a nationality, there a nationality, here a settlement of Germans, there one of Austrians!, there one of Slavis, there one of Swedes, there one of Norwegians? That is the problem. Every man in this House from western Canada knows that the largest problem that lies before us is the assimilation of our races and the development' of national efficiency. They	all	know	it. There	is	not aman who studies the question who does	not	know	it, and	I	appeal
to the common sense, I appeal to the patriotism of this House, in this time of stress and pain, not to permit it to be thought that we hold out hopes to these [DOT]people settling on the plains that there shall be federal interference for the purpose of promoting the growth of little nationalities in this great Confederation.
I should like to tell you some of the perils that are now being experienced in Saskatchewan, some of the evils that are creeping in there by reason of this very thing, and of the splendid efforts that are being made to overcome them or grapple with them. The situation is being faced with the dauntless energy with which men are throwing themselves into the heroic task of assimilating this vast cosmopolitan population; but all this effort fails, all these labours will be in vain, if this Parliament, speaking for the people of the Dominion, not realizing the measure of its responsibilities, says to these new citizens: "If your legislature does thus and so, we will tell them that we want this thing changed and fixed so that you will have a continuation of your national existence."
Sir, at this time of the night I have no right to trespass upon the time of this House, but I should like to summarize my position, speaking, like the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), as one from the West, in these words:
I believe in the maintenance of our Constitution. I believe that the series of compromises that made possible the passing of the British North America Act embodying legislation protecting the rights and privileges of minorities, were wisely made by the Fathers of Confederation. I believe that under that constitutional system, by which plenary powers were given to the legislatures of the provinces to enact laws with relation to education without interference by this Parliament, is- to be found the safest and the surest possible remedy for the differ-
ences and difficulties that we experience in the growth of national sentiment in this great democracy. I go further: I believe that it is wholly unconstitutional, wholly irrelevant, for this Parliament at this time to be endeavouring to interfere with this matter. I am not concerned with what may be done in these provinces, except in so far as there may be a violation by them of the constitutional powers which have been committed to them; and, if I may appeal to the common sense, to the patriotism, and to the reason of this House, to the men of the East, and especially to the men of Quebec, may I say to
them,	in the language of my hon. friend who has .just taken his seat, that nothing could be more dangerous for Quebec than to have it thought that this issue is thrust upon this House at this time, looking towards the coercion of another province, for the advantage of a minority that comes from that province. In my province, where 30,000 men have rushed to the colours, the talk that has already been engendered by reason of this legislation is something to be reckoned with. It makes for bad feeling, it makes for discontent, it makes for lack of harmony, and in the end for the disturbance and destruction of the state. I should like to remind this House, and especially my friends from the province of Quebec who referred to the naturalization laws, that if they lived in the United States they would find that the influence which they exercised upon the body politic would be limited as it is in the New England states, as compared with what it is here under the splendid constitution, which guarantees them a fixed representation in this Parliament and the preservation of their rights, privileges, and liberties. The very debates which I hold in' my hand contain a statement by Sir George Cartier in which he pointed out that if once there be an interference by this Parliament with the free rights of the provinces to pass educational legislation,
then,	as he said, " The rights of my French compatriots in Quebec may one day be interfered with by a Protestant Parliament." So that I do again appeal to them to reflect, to pause, to consider, before they place themselves upon record as being opposed to the doctrine which their fathers who laid the foundations of this Confederation thought right, proper and just. I have no doubt, as a friend of mine said to me tonight, that if the question were only dis-

cussed between some of us who come from the other provinces with some who come from Quebec, much might have been gained, in the way of remedying the grievance if there be a grievance. But when a province endeavours to speak as a whole, when the mass of the population headed and guided by one who for 40 years has sat in this Parliament, then indeed, I say it is evil they do and not good. I am as certain of that as that I stand here this night. Nothing but evil can come from anything that makes the united effort of the great mass of a province project itself against the rights of another piovince. As individuals we love, we admire, we reverence those who come from the province of Quebec. Our relations have always been most happy and harmonious, and always will be; but it is one thing to deal with the individual and with the pressure that a combination of individuals may exercise in the way I have indicated; an effort combined under the leadership of one who for 40 years has sat in this* Parliament and who, as he told us, has been a leader of the Liberal party for 28 years, in good report and ill report is another thing. It is quite another thing for one who leads a great party to ask for the destruction of the rights of a province as they were laid down by the founders of Confederation. In the name of unity of purpose, of harmony, of the greatness of the Dominion that is to be, remember those great plains that are to be peopled by millions, and that one day will say to my friends from Quebec:	" We
have not forgotten your efforts." I would deprecate it, and so would others; but let this country realize, as my hon. friend from Edmonton said, that the shifting of population is already in progress. It will not be in my day possibly; it will not he in the day possibly of any one in this House, but as certain as the sun shines, those great lands between the lakes and the mountains will have a population as great as that which inhabits the central west of the United States. It will have reached 150,000,000 within a reasonable time and I am perfectly convinced that these 50,000,000 living under the protecting aegis of the Union Jack, as British subjects, securing to them liberty and justice and freedom; securing them from the tyranny of minorities which may be greater than the tyranny of majorities-that must not he forgotten, it is a fact in history-securing them from
that, we will, if we are true to the trust that devolves upon us, leave to them a country whose institutions make possible the development of that unity of purpose, that harmony of feeling, that intelligent coordination of effort that brings about national efficiency under one language of communication and instruction which, in this case, must be, because we are part and parcel of the British Empire, the English language.

Mr. Speaker, at this very late hour of the night I owe an apology to the House for attempting to address it at all. But for the impassioned harangue of the hon. gentleman who has just sat down, and who has introduced a note into this debate somewhat out of touch with the high plane on which the discussion has been carried on by other hon. gentlemen, I would not have ventured to trespass upon your patience, and I shall do so only for a few moments. When my hon. friend from Calgary, with that assertiveness which he can command with very little justification, says that my hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Pardee) misled this House in regard to what took place in this Parliament in 1872, it would not be proper to permit this debate to close without showing conclusively to the House that my hon. friend from Calgary is the one who has attempted to mislead the House. When was it ever said in this or any other Parliament that when a matter for the House had passed a resolution and determined that a certain thing should .be done, it was a question as to how the matter had Ibeen brought to the attention of the House. My hon. friend laid down a very curious doctrine. I am sure that you, Mr. Speaker, never heard of it before. Because in 1872 a certain matter was brought to the attention of this House by virtue of a resolution moved by Mt. Oostigan, in which after certain recitals, this House was asked to come to the conclusion that a certain Act of the Province of New Brunswick *should be disallowed, and because that resolution was amended and the House came to a subsequent conclusive resolution as the result of debate, my hon. friend from Calgary says that my hon. friend from Lambton misled the House when he told the House what the result was which Parliament arrived at.

That was not the
resolution.

.My hon. friend will find that in his hasty way of looking at this question he has not seen all the books upon the subject. My hon. friend will find on page 179 of the Journals of the House of 1872 the following statement:
Then the main question, as amended, being put, that this House regrets that the School Act recently passed in New Brunswick is unsatisfactory to a portion of the inhabitants of that Province, and hopes that it may be so modified during the next session of the Legislature of New Brunswick as to remove any just grounds of discontent that now exist.
That was the resolution quoted by my hon. friend from Lambton.

Pardon me: I must correct my hon. friend at once. The resolution quoted by the hon. member for Lambton is on page 177 and is the resolution that Mr. Colby moved. The resolution on page 179, which was passed, was not moved by Mr. Colby because it involved two amendments.

My hon. friend is certainly indulging in very queer reasoning. On page 177 I find that Mr. Colby moved a resolution in the very words which were read by .my hon. friend from Lambton, which I read a moment ago, and which afterwards formed part of the main resolution. Does my hon. friend from Calgary want this House to believe that it was misled when I read the same words on page 179, where, after the words, "Then, the main question, as amended, being put," are to be found the very words contained in the resolution of Mr. Colby, and then, after adding the substantive resolution, the record says:	"it was resolved
in the affirmative." The fact therefore is that in 1872, as recorded on page 179 of the Journals of that year, the House of Commons passed a resolution which contained the words exactly as read by my hon. friend from Lamibton. In 1875 this question came before - Parliament again. My hon. friend read what the Hon. Mr. Blake said in regard to the matter at that period. Let me tell my hon. friend that <in 1875 the Hon. Edward Blake seconded a resolution, moved by Mr. Cauchon and dealing with .this very question of New Brunswick schools. It had no relation to the legislation which my hon. friend conjured up, but was a legitimate and apparently natural sequence to the resolution moved in 1872. For the information of the House, in view of the statement made by my hon. friend from Calgary, I wish

.to read this resolution which was moved by Mr. Cauchon and seconded by Mr. Blake in 1875, and I want this House to judge whether my hon. friend from Lambton was right when he read the resolution of 1872, or whether my hon. friend from Calgary was right. This is the resolution of 1875:	'
Mr. Cauehon moved, in amendment to the said proposed amendment, seconded by Mr. Blake, That the words "That on the 29th day of May, 1872, the House of Commons adopted the following Resolution.
This House regrets that the School Act recently passed in New Brunswick, is unsatisfactory to a portion of the inhabitants of that province, and hopes that it may be so modified during the next session of the legislature of New Brunswick as to remove any just ground of discontent that now exists.
There are the words that my hon. friend from Lambton read. Messrs. Cauchon and Blake, in 1875, refer to this resolution of 1872 in the terms of the following motion:
This House regrets that the hope expressed in the said resolution has not been realized.
That an humble address be presented to Her Most Gracious Majesty the Queen, embodying this resolution, and praying that Her Majesty would he graciously pleased to use her influence with the legislature of New Brunswick to procure such a modification of the said Act, as shall remove such grounds of discontent.
We thus have the resolution of 1875 quoting the very words read by my hon. friend from Lambton to-night and when the hon. member for Calgary, at this hour in the morning, and in such a debate as this, has the assurance to charge one of his colleagues with having made a false statement I say that he has not the right to do it, and that he has no right to trespass upon a debate of this kind for such a purpose. My hon. friend talks about the great West with his usual eloquence, but he knows just as well as every lawyer in this House that this resolution has no bearing whatever, directly or indirectly, on Alberta, Saskatchewan, British Columbia, or any other province in this Dominion except Ontario. My hon. friend knows full well that by a resolution which was pressed in this House by a former Minister of Public Works, the Hon. Mr. Monk, in 1905, it was proposed to create certain rights in Alberta and Saskatchewan with respect to the use of the French language and that my right hon. leader at' that time, dealing with th^t question frankly and fairly, called upon his followers to vote down that resolution. It was voted down, and my hon. friend knows that to-day, when he talks about the interference with the English language in Alberta and Saskatchewan, he is talking

beside the mark. No such question can arise there.
Just one word on the general question. Those of us who speak the English tongue, those of us who treasure the memories of the great British race during all the long years of the history of our Empire, must realize that the foundations of the race and of the Empire were laid by men of various races, Angles, Saxons, Jutes, and Normans, who came over to England. These men spoke a number of different languages. In the North, and across the channel in Ireland, were the Celts, while in Wales there were the men of the Cymric race. By a consideration of the varying and conflicting interests of the ipeople, and not by acts of hostility, not by speeches such as my hon. friend from Calgary delivered here to-night, but through long years of harmonizing these difficulties and of working together, there grew up the great British race to which we are all so proud to belong, which laid the foundations of our Empire and which carried the British flag to every sea. Whenever a race came under that flag what did they do? Wherever the flag was planted the first essential right that was recognized of the people who came under their government was the right to the language of the people who lived in that land. So the story has come down all through the years. What has occurred in South Africa? After the war, lured by the assurances of the 'Germans, there trekked up into German territory a great number of Boers. They found an illustration there of the difference between British and German rule, because the Germans enforced the principle of uniformity of languages and the subordination of the rights of the Boers to the dominance of the Germans. These men found their way back to British territory, and under the British flag, where the right of their language was accorded to them, and to-day we have the spectacle of the .whole of Africa being saved to the Empire as a result of the recognition of the rights of these Boers to their language in South Africa. When we come to Canada, I know that gentlemen like the hon. member foT Calgary tell us that we must have one language in this land from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
I did not say that.

I did not say that my hon. friend said it; I said gentlemen like my hon. friend. We have heard that, and it is a very pleasant thing to say in
certain quarters. Men of the dominant race will say we should have one country, with one language, that we should have one flag, and there should be no exception to that proposition. But, we in Canada, are fettered in regard to that matter. We do not control this question of language. Those of the class to which I have referred, like to say there should be only one language in Canada.	But that cannot be the
case. Why?-because Imperial enactments and treaties have provided conditions in this country by which men of the French race who were here when our fathers came are given in the courts, and in the province of Quebec certain rights and privileges that can never be taken away. Not only in this Parliament can a man come from any part of this Dominion 'Speaking the French language, representing people who speak that language and having the right to expect that a gentleman shall sit in the Speaker's chair who shall know what is being said when he addresses him on behalf of those who elected him to Parliament, but in the Supreme Court any man who speaks the French language has the right to demand that his plaint shall be heard by a court composed of men who 'Understand the French language. You have the Exchequer Court, which travels from the Atlantic to the Pacific under Judge Cassells and under Judge Audette. Every litigant in this country can hire a counsel who does not understand one word of English, under the law created by the Imperial Parliament, he has a right to have his plaint heard.
When may hon. friend talks about conditions in this country, when he talks as if the men of the French race, whose rights are embalmed in the constitution under which we live, are to be told that there is only to be one race in Canada, he must remember that whatever we would like to do, whatever individuals might desire, the hands of the Canadian Parliament and of the Canadian people are indelibly fettered by reason of these conditions imposed by the British Parliament and by the conditions under which our constitution arose. That being so, what are we going to do in this land? Are we to be continually aggressors against each other? Is it by preaohing such a doctrine that we are going to attain that peace and unity which are so essential to the upbuilding and the future of this country? Is it by preaching division amongst these races that this unity is to be had? No problem with regard to the French



language in the schools arises in any of the provinces of this Dominion except Quebec, Ontario and Manitoba? And why does it arise in Manitoba? Simply and solely because in 1897 this Parliament chose to create certain Tights in that province, which created a 'condition from which you cannot get away. But in all the other provinces of the Dominion than these three there iis no restriction, no danger, for those who worry in regard to this question. The legislatures of every one of our provinces except Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba have absolute, supreme and exclusive rights in regard to every question of education, and this Parliament cannot interfere in any way with those rights, and it does not propose to interfere. What is our situation here? This resolution is not an invasion of provincial rights. This Parliament does not in any way intend to interfere with provincial jurisdiction. On the contrary, it expressly recognizes it. 'Hon. gentlemen in this House who have spoken in this debate, no matter from which side of the House, have all admitted that there is an agitation and there are grievances. Some hon. gentlemen opposite have spoken most admirably on this question, notably the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle), who dealt with it in a way that was most interesting to those of us from other provinces who were anxious to know the facts. He declared that the people of Ontario were anxious to encourage the teaching of French as well as the teaching of English, and that they believed these regulations would effect that purpose. Hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, in utterances which were notably clear, and free from all passion and prejudice, placed before this Parliament statements which indicated that the rights and privileges of the men of the French race which existed before Confederation, and have since been recognized by statute and regulation in Ontario, have been interfered with and abridged. What is to be done? My hon. friend says, " Let this matter go to the Privy Council and be litigated upon." Is there not a better way in which we can arrive at a full and complete understanding on this question? This House is in a splendid temper, a temper I have rarely seen equalled during all my parliamentary experience. This question has been presented fairly and equitably from both sides, and is it not reason-
able and natural to expect this Parliament, forgetting all questions of party, to say: If we have in Canada these conditions, everybody should recognize them, and so far as we can, we should model ourselves on the lines laid down by the Imperial Parliament; and both racks should go along under this Constitution in amity and friendship. That is the proposition which is made to this House. That is all that is asked for by the mover of the resolution. Realizing to the full that Ontario is supreme on this question, and without any desire to restrict her rights by any legislative action, all we say is that if there are grievances there-should be a rehearing of the case, and an investigation of all the facts, and we would then leave it to the good sense of the people of the province of Ontario to recognize the rights that exist, and deal fairly by all classes of the population. That is the intent and meaning of the resolution presented by the hon. member for Kamouraska. If it meant an invasion of provincial rights I should be the first to vote against it, but there is no desire to invade or attack the supremacy of Ontario. All that is asked is a rehearing, full and fair consideration of the exact conditions, free from prejudice. That and that alone is what is sought by this resolution, and I trust that when this question is taken up by the Legislature of Ontario which alone can deal with it, the men who control Ontario and its educational policy will realize these conditions and endeavour to deal with this question fairly and equitably; that the cause of difference between the races of this country may be removed, and the difficulty settled along lines which are just and equitable, and characteristic of the British fair play which we of the British race have boasted of through all the years of our history.

(Chicoutimi-Saguenay) (Translation.) Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding the lateness of the hour, I wish to give some explanation of the stand I intend to take on the question now before this House. I wish also to express in my mother tongue the opinion I have formed after perusing the whole of the debate in which the House has been engaged for the last two days. I think a little French, on this question of French, may not be out of place.
The resolution now before the House expresses the unanimous sentiment of every Canadian-be he French or English speaking-because it is a well-known fact that

under the folds of the British flag, of which we are so proud, every subject enjoys the greatest possible measure of freedom-; what is going on in the province of Quebec is the best instance.
But in certain of the- provinces of the Dominion, educational laws have been enacted, in good faith I presume, which are more or less unsatisfactory to the French Canadians. In the resolution which has now taken two days to discuss, Ontario only has been taken to task for enacting, on the subject of education, laws which are not as complete as they should -be. We are all agreed that we must join in an endeavour to obtain the redress of grievances, whatever and wherever they be. I heard no word of dissent as to that. The time has come when the law makers are willing to take action under the law and the constitution.
In Ontario, as I have just stated, there exists a statute which is insufficient as regards French Canadians; but in Manitoba, there was a statute which was also insufficient, but which, such as it was, had been giving our compatriots for some years past a certain measure of satisfaction. Well, a few weeks ago, the Government of that province saw fit to call on the legislature to repeal that statute and, at one fell blow, to deprive the French population of all the privileges they had enjoyed hitherto.
We are appealed to on behalf of the wounded of Ontario, but what about our murdered brethren of Manitoba? Do we really believe that in the latter province so heavy has been the blow that all remedy is hopeless and 'we must be resigned to have the case buried for evermore? That is the conclusion that may be drawn from our two days' debate. If Parliament is entitled to discuss my hon. friend's resolution was it not open to us a few weeks ago, while the Ontario and Manitoba Legislatures were both in session, to submit at both capitals with some chance of success the humble prayer which this House to-day is asked to formulate? But now tjhere is behind the present resolution no possible sanction, and at any rate any chance of 'better conditions is retarded a whole year by the delay in presenting such a resolution.
Would it not have yet been time, before the Manitoba guillotine severed whatever rights remained to us in that province, for the promoter of this resolution, by some such measure, to urge on the provincial Prime Minister before letting the knife

drop, the desirability of giving a second thought, to ponder over what is legitimate and what is right, and perhaps instil into him some feeling of pity towards our compatriots? Far easier to forestall death than to resurrect. Would it not then have been the part of wisdom to suggest to the Manitoba Government some action along the lines of this resolution; then might have been avoided the massacre of the French race in Manitoba and might have been obtained in Ontario the balance of those rights to which I believe the French 'Canadians are entitled.
Mr. MARCI'L:	Will the hon. member
allow me a question? Why did not the hon.. member himself introduce a resolution to that effect?
Why not have inserted if in the present resolution?

If the Government allows me to introduce such -a resolution, because as my hon. friend well knows, the rules of the House forbid a second amendment,- but if the Government will consent to suspend the rules, I shall immediately move a resolution, which I shall ask my hon. friend to second.

I am ready to do anything that is required of me, in order that what is not right may be made so. Like you, I am a French Canadian; like you I am a staunch believer; I have a wife and children; I am a Catholic, and I' represent a constituency which is Catholic and Frenchspeaking just like yours. But I wish to know why by taking a very skillful advantage of the rules of the House, we have been precluded from having a regular amendment put to us, when it could have been done in the regular course, if this resolution had not been moved in amendment to a motion that the House go into Supply.
I admit, without hesitation, that we have come to a difficult juncture in our national history, when all fair-minded men, all who feel their responsibilities, should unite in an effort to avert the danger with which we are threatened.
But what reason have we to deal to-day with the schools in Ontario only, where French is being commonly taught, and leaving out of consideration the people of Manitoba, from whom everything has been taken away? Is there a secret motive? Along with my colleagues, I am hound by my oath of office, by my allegiance to my language, my faith and my religion, to de-

vote all my energies to see that the rights of all are respected, especially the rights of minorities. I have laboured alongside men, much higher than I, to help the wounded .of Ontario and on behalf of the murdered ones of Manitoba, whom I would bring back to life. Accordingly, I much regret that the resolution which is submitted to us falls so short of what it should contain, and is so unfair as regards those of our compatriots who are suffering the more painful agony, and that the amendment should have come before us through a procedure that precludes its being amended to put it in a more acceptable form, and gives it practically the character of a motion of censure on the Government.
I expected to see the Government censured for not having disallowed the Ontario statute, but I was surprised to hear the chieftains of the Opposition, especially the leader, speak against the principle of disallowance. What purpose did it serve them to trouble so many peaceful citizens all over the country to get them to petition for disallowance, when it must have been known that it was impossible under the circumstances? Why not have introduced the present resolution as a substantive motion that could have been discussed with the same good faith as we are doing now, and modified, if necessary, to make it more comprehensive instead of limited in scope, as is the amendment before us?
Mr. Speaker, I repeat what I have just said; we have arrived at a terrible chapter of our annals. Had we not enough on our hands with the abominable war that shakes the world to its very foundations? We are now threatened with a civil war, necessarily brought about by an injustice which, as I understand, depends on a mere word in a regulation. At the present juncture, knowing the danger of the agitation that is being promoted, I feel it is my duty to appeal to the wisdom of the fair-minded men of both parties in this House and out of this House, to join in an attempt to ward off this menace, and as soon as possible reestablish peace in our great Dominion.
With the present widespread perturbation, I should suggest that new men, independent of the present organization, get together and endeavour to bring about a redress of the grievances complained of by peaceful and diplomatic means, which alone will bring back to Canada the quiet it enjoyed heretofore.
In closing, I want it clearly understood that I am, from a sense of duty as well as

by common sense, intent on working along with all broad-minded citizens against the perpetration of any wrong; I am as loyal to my race as any of my colleagues and countrymen; I desire to give all my endeavours to .secure a remedy for the grievances in Ontario, and especially in Manitoba, but I do not think the resolution before the House expresses these sentiments with any greater force than the declarations I have just made.
I profoundly deplore that the murder of the rights of my compatriots in Manitoba should not have been covered by the resolution, but I hope that the discussion of the last two days will prompt fair-minded men of all classes to go to work and see that permanent justice be granted to those to whom their rights are now denied.
With these words I must state that while I support heart and soul the sentiments expressed in the resolution, I feel that I cannot vote for it on the grounds that it overlooks the rights of a section of out compatriots, because it is too limited in its scope, because it has no sanction behind it, and because, as put before the House, it amounts to a non-confidence motion against the Government, without assigning any reasons therefor.

(Maskinonge)
(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, in the province of Ontario, as we are made to understand, strong condemnation is being expressed in certain quarters against our intervention and our protests in connection with the rights of the French Canadian minority in that province.
In this vast Dominion, if one province is guilty of a very great wrong, such as is apt to disturb the harmony between the races that make up the country's population, it seems to me that it is permissible for this Parliament or for a sister province to record some comments, or make suggestions, without being accused of any disloyalty, or of a desire to dominate. The part of a legislator is to maintain here below peace, justice, and truth.
The world war, which is now being waged, is without doubt the outcome bf injustices similar to those which are to-day perpetrated in the province of Ontario.
In defiance of all right, our schools may be taken away from us, but never will anyone succeed in extirpating from our bosom our French hearts, no more than we should attempt to instil in the heart of an Irishman, an Orangeman, or a Scotchman, our

French ideals, and national aspirations. It the country is to have peace and prosperity, why not be respectful of our mutual rights?
The claim is heard that the Gospel can' be preached and taught in the one language:	what an error! What folly! Are
we not aware that the Gospel is taught both in Catholic and Protestant churches, in this country and elsewhere, in the language of the people? Was not the gift of tongues bestowed on Peter, the Apostle of Christ, so that his teachings might be understood by all the nations of the world? Alas! that a priest, a Catholic bishop, should be so blind as to make common cause with the Orangemen in their attacks upon our race. Does he not realize that the interests of religion, the welfare of the country, the promotion of peace in Canada, forbid him to assail a minority that has acquired rights and shows respect for his high office?
See what is going on in the province of Quebec; there the Protestant minority enjoys the full control of its school grants, and the use of its language not only in its churches, but also in its educational institutions.
It is objected that we are only a handful. A handful, indeed, when the minority accounts for nearly 250,000 French Canadians ! And what if it were true? Not the units and not their wealth give the measure of moral energy. After all, might does not make right, and has not the spectacle been given to the world of twelve apostles, whom we all revere, although despised by all the wealth, the pride and the science of their time, conquering the world.
I do not look forward to our conquering North America, but I claim that justice calls for respect, even when the number of its exponents is insignificant. The brutal element in a wrong is not capable of turning it into a right.
The idea of having only one language spoken in Ontario is a sham and a utopia. It may as well be realized immediately that never will the revindication of our rights be silenced, because the French language was spoken in Ontario long before it was settled by a British majority. In Europe, with the French soldier always pushing forward on the battlefield and the English host never falling back, victory will finally settle with the Allies; likewise in Ontario, where the French Canadian will never give up the rights he has acquired and the fair-minded and honest British
who does not recede, we finally will get the majority in this province to understand the respect due to the minority. The different factions who are attacking the French language will give in at last, justice will triumph, because no language has played a nobler part in the world's destinies, in the triumph of civilization in Europe and Canada. It is spoken in all the courts, sovereigns learn it, speak it, and are not ashamed of it. Mr. Speaker, I could speak longer on the beauties of the French language, and the rights of the minority to continue its use in this province; but on account of the late hour, I conclude in stating that my remarks are founded on justice, that they are made on behalf of my province, and of the minority in Ontario. In giving expression to my opinion, I believe I voice the sentiments of all those who wish for peace, justice, harmony, not only in the province of Quebec, but also in the province of Ontario and all the other provinces of the Dominion. I shall then vote for the amendment of the hon. member for Kamouraska.
